items.q: What is the size of the torque from push 1 about the hinge? Give the value and its unit.

mistakes.why: Value: that divides the force by the distance. Torque is lever arm × force.
Value: that uses 0.40 m. Push 1 acts at the edge, 0.80 m from the hinge.

why.correct: Push 1 is perpendicular to the door, so its lever arm is the full 0.80 m: τ = r⊥F = (0.80 m)(30 N) = 24 N·m.

items.q: Rank the sizes of the torques the four pushes exert about the hinge.
options: τ₁ > τ₂ = τ₃ > τ₄
τ₁ = τ₃ > τ₂ > τ₄
τ₁ = τ₂ = τ₃ = τ₄
τ₄ > τ₁ > τ₃ > τ₂

why.correct: Lever arms: push 1, 0.80 m; push 2, 0.40 m; push 3, (0.80 m)(sin 30°) = 0.40 m; push 4, 0. With F = 30 N: 24, 12, 12 and 0 N·m.
options: Right: 24, 12, 12 and 0 N·m.
Push 3 acts at the edge but at 30°, so its lever arm is halved to 0.40 m.
Equal forces give equal torques only with equal lever arms.
Push 4 points straight at the hinge, so its lever arm is zero.

items.q: Why does push 4 produce no torque about the hinge?
options: Its line of action passes through the hinge
It is weaker than the other three pushes
It acts at the point farthest from the hinge
The door’s weight cancels it

why.correct: Torque is r⊥F, where r⊥ is the perpendicular distance from the axis to the force’s line of action. Push 4 points along the door straight at the hinge, so r⊥ = 0 and τ = 0, however hard the push.
options: Right: the perpendicular distance from the hinge to its line is zero.
All four pushes are 30 N; the difference is the lever arm.
Pushes 1 and 3 act there too and do give torques.
The door’s weight is vertical; push 4 is horizontal along the door. They do not cancel, and neither is the reason.

items.q: What is the size of the torque from push 3 about the hinge?

mistakes.why: Value: that uses cos 30°. The angle is between the door (r) and the force, so τ = rF sin θ.
Value: that ignores the 30° angle. Only the part of the push perpendicular to the door turns it.

why.correct: τ = rF sin θ = (0.80 m)(30 N)(sin 30°) = 12 N·m. Equivalently, the lever arm is (0.80 m)(sin 30°) = 0.40 m.

items.q: Push 2 is moved to the outer edge of the door and its force is halved to 15 N, still perpendicular to the door. Its torque about the hinge is now
options: the same as before
twice as large
half as large
four times as large
Right: twice the lever arm × half the force = same torque.
The force is halved, which cancels the doubled lever arm.
The lever arm doubles, which cancels the halved force.
Torque is the product r⊥F: (2)(½) = 1.

items.q: Counterclockwise is positive. What is the torque of the 20 N force about the axle, with its sign?

mistakes.why: Value: that divides the force by the distance. τ = r⊥F.

why.correct: The 20 N force pushes down left of the axle, turning the bar counterclockwise: τ = +(0.30 m)(20 N) = +6.0 N·m.

items.q: Counterclockwise is positive. What is the net torque on the bar about the axle?

mistakes.why: Value: that adds every torque as positive. The 15 N force turns the bar clockwise, so its torque is negative.
Value: that gives the 10 N upward force a clockwise torque. Pulling up right of the axle turns the bar counterclockwise.

why.correct: +6.0 N·m (20 N, counterclockwise) − 6.0 N·m (15 N, clockwise) + 2.0 N·m (10 N up on the right, counterclockwise) = +2.0 N·m.

items.q: The bar starts at rest. Which way does it begin to turn?
options: Counterclockwise, because the net torque is counterclockwise
Clockwise, because two of the three forces push down
It stays still, because the 20 N and 15 N torques cancel
Clockwise, because the 15 N force is farthest from the axle

why.correct: Sum the torques with signs: +6.0 − 6.0 + 2.0 = +2.0 N·m. A nonzero net torque starts the bar turning in its direction, counterclockwise.
options: Right: the net torque is +2.0 N·m.
Pushing down turns the bar one way on the left of the axle and the other way on the right; count torques, not forces.
Those two do cancel, but the 10 N force still gives a +2.0 N·m torque.
Its torque, 6.0 N·m, is the same size as the 20 N force’s torque.

items.q: The bar is 0.90 m long, so its right end is 0.45 m from the axle. Which single extra force, perpendicular to the bar at its right end, makes the net torque zero?
options: 4.4 N down
4.4 N up
2.0 N down
0.90 N down

why.correct: The extra force must give −2.0 N·m: pushing down right of the axle is clockwise, and F = 2.0 N·m ÷ 0.45 m = 4.44 N, about 4.4 N.
options: Right: a clockwise torque of 2.0 N·m = (0.45 m)F.
Pulling up on the right end adds counterclockwise torque; the bar already has too much.
This sets the force equal to the torque. Divide the torque by the lever arm.
This multiplies the torque by the lever arm instead of dividing.

items.q: The lever arm of a force about an axis is
options: the perpendicular distance from the axis to the force’s line of action
the distance from the axis to where the force acts
the length of the force arrow
the distance from the force to the center of mass

why.correct: Extend the force along its line of action. The lever arm r⊥ is the perpendicular distance from the axis to that line; τ = r⊥F.
options: Right: r⊥, the shortest distance from the axis to the line.
That is r. The lever arm is r⊥ = r sin θ, which equals r for a perpendicular force.
The arrow’s length shows the force’s size, not a distance.
Torque is about the chosen axis, not the center of mass.

items.q: A mechanic pulls on the end of a 0.30 m wrench with an 80 N force at 60° to the handle. What is the size of the torque about the bolt?

mistakes.why: Value: that uses cos 60°. τ = rF sin θ, with θ the angle between the handle and the force.
Value: that ignores the angle; that is the torque of a perpendicular pull.

why.correct: τ = rF sin θ = (0.30 m)(80 N)(sin 60°) = 20.8 N·m, about 21 N·m.

items.q: How does a force diagram of a beam differ from a free-body diagram of the beam?
options: Each force is drawn from the point where it acts on the beam
Each force is drawn from a dot at the center of mass
Each force is split into parts along and across the beam
The net torque is drawn as an extra curved arrow

why.correct: A free-body diagram puts all forces at one dot. For rotation the point of application matters, so a force diagram draws the object and starts each force where it acts, labelled with type and agent.
options: Right: torques depend on where forces act, so the diagram shows it.
That is a free-body diagram; it hides where forces act, so it cannot show torques.
Both diagrams show whole forces; components go beside the diagram.
Neither diagram shows a net force or net torque as an extra arrow.

items.q: A bolt is stuck. With the least force, how should you push on the wrench?
options: Perpendicular to the handle, at its far end
Perpendicular to the handle, near the bolt
Along the handle, toward the bolt
At 30° to the handle, at its far end

why.correct: For a fixed torque, F = τ/r⊥. The lever arm is largest when the force is perpendicular to the handle at the far end, so the force needed is smallest.
options: Right: the largest lever arm gives a given torque with the smallest force.
A small lever arm needs a large force for the same torque.
A push along the handle has zero lever arm and no torque.
The lever arm is then halved, so you need twice the force.

items.q: A bolt needs a torque of 45 N·m to loosen. A wrench is 0.30 m long. What perpendicular force at its end is needed?

mistakes.why: Value: that multiplies torque by length. F = τ/r⊥.

items.q: A force of fixed size acts at the end of a wrench. The angle between the handle and the force changes from 90° to 30°. The torque
options: halves
stays the same
falls to one third
doubles

why.correct: τ = rF sin θ. sin 90° = 1 and sin 30° = 0.5, so the torque falls to half.
options: Right: sin 30° = 0.5, so the lever arm halves.
The force and r are the same, but the lever arm r sin θ shrinks.
Torque follows sin θ, not θ itself: sin 30°/sin 90° = 0.5.
Tilting the force away from perpendicular reduces the torque.

items.q: Counterclockwise is positive. A force that would start a wheel turning clockwise exerts a torque that is
options: negative
positive
zero
positive or negative, depending on its size

why.correct: On this exam a torque is described only as clockwise or counterclockwise. With counterclockwise positive, any torque tending to turn the object clockwise is negative.
options: Right: the sign of a torque says which way it tends to turn the object.
Positive was chosen as counterclockwise.
A force that starts the wheel turning has a nonzero torque.
The sign comes from the direction of turning, not the size.
